HexagonGuide.strategyTitle: Tips — how you memorize decides it
HexagonGuide.strategyIntro: In the final, memory and composure mattered more than arithmetic. Common approaches:

strategies.title: Chunk the rows
strategies.body: Remember rows as chunks like '163' and '2456', the way you would a phone number. 19 tiles fit in 30 seconds more easily.

strategies.title: Pre-add some lines
strategies.body: You cannot add all 27 lines, but knowing the sums of the 9 across-lines lets you call some answers as soon as the target shows.

strategies.title: The centre tile J is in 6 lines
strategies.body: The middle tile is used by the most lines. Make sure of the central numbers before the edges.

strategies.title: A wrong answer erases a right one
strategies.body: With +1 and −1, a half-sure guess loses on average. The show's analysis that avoiding wrong calls matters most was right.

strategies.title: Easy ones first

TwoSidedPokerGuide.title: Two-Sided Poker — front or back, where do your chips go?
TwoSidedPokerGuide.intro: Two-Sided Poker is the 1v1 chip survival known from the Grand Final death match of The Genius: Black Garnet. Each card has two numbers: everyone sees the front, only you see the back. Reading which face to play, and which face your opponent will pick, is the whole game. PUZZLTHINK uses the Grand Final rules against an Easy, Normal or Hard AI, or a friend.
rules: Both players start with 40 chips and ante 1 each hand. Lose all your chips and you lose.
The deck has 50 cards whose two faces differ in parity, four sets of each (200 cards). Fronts are public; only the owner sees the back.
The first player picks front or back and bets; the other picks a face and calls, raises or folds. On a call both cards are shown and the bigger chosen number wins.
A two-sided bet costs double and wins only if both of your numbers beat the face your opponent chose. A tie loses. A win takes 10 extra chips.
Folding to a two-sided bet still pays 10 chips. Ties carry the pot to the next hand's winner.

special.title: Card counting
special.body: Cards dealt from the 200-card shoe never come back. Remember them to narrow down your opponent's back face.

special.title: Parity
special.body: A card's two faces always differ in parity: an even front means an odd back.

special.title: Three AI levels
special.body: Easy, Normal and Hard aim at roughly 80%, 50% and 25% player wins. Hard counts cards and watches betting patterns.

special.title: Friends, open matches and replays
special.body: Play a friend 1v1 with a link or a 4-digit code, or join an open match. Afterwards, replay each hand to see where it turned.

TwoSidedPokerGuide.strategyIntro: Two-Sided Poker is a fight over information, not numbers.

strategies.title: Play your bigger face
strategies.body: Picking your bigger number is the default, which is exactly why a well-timed bluff on the smaller face can work.

strategies.title: Start from their front
strategies.body: A big front usually means they'll play it. A small front may mean they trust their back.

strategies.title: Go two-sided only when sure
strategies.body: It pays only when both numbers are high, and a tie loses, so a single face is safer when in doubt.

strategies.title: Manage your stack
strategies.body: As the pot grows, folding can be the cheap option. Watch the chip gap and avoid forced raises.

faq.q: Which show is Two-Sided Poker from?
faq.a: It appeared as a death match and in the Grand Final of The Genius: Black Garnet. PUZZLTHINK uses the Grand Final rules.

SlitherlinkGuide.title: Slitherlink — how to draw the loop
SlitherlinkGuide.intro: Slitherlink is a logic puzzle played on a grid of dots: draw a single unbroken loop. A number in a cell says how many of its four sides the loop runs along. PUZZLTHINK makes a fresh board with exactly one answer every time.
rules: Only neighbouring dots can be joined, across or down. No diagonals.
All lines must join into one closed loop: no branches (three lines at a dot) and no loose ends.
A numbered cell has exactly that many of its sides on the loop.
Cells without a number have no limit.
Practice offers 9×9, 10×10 and 11×11 (show size) dot boards, with unlimited hints.

special.title: Pen
special.body: Tap between two neighboring dots to draw a line. Tap the same spot again to clear it (line ↔ empty), or drag to draw every edge you cross in one stroke (starting on a line erases). A ✕ only goes down with the ✕ button. Undo, or Ctrl/⌘+Z, steps back one change at a time.

special.title: Eraser · Clear all
special.body: Tap a line or ✕ with the eraser to remove it. Clear all needs two taps, and lines from hints stay.

special.title: Marker ✕
special.body: Leave a small ✕ on sides you know are empty. It does not affect the answer; it is a note for yourself.

special.title: Hint · Give up · Replay
special.body: Press hint, then tap the board: the answer for the 3×3 dots around it is filled in. Giving up draws the answer loop, and you can replay your own lines step by step.

SlitherlinkGuide.strategyIntro: Fill in what is certain first and the rest follows.

strategies.title: Start with 0s
strategies.body: Mark all four sides of a 0 with ✕. A 3 next to a 0 uses its other three sides.

strategies.title: 3s and 1s in corners
strategies.body: A 3 in a corner uses both outer sides; a 1 in a corner uses neither.

strategies.title: Two 3s side by side
strategies.body: Two adjacent 3s use the side between them and both far sides.

strategies.title: Zero or two lines per dot
strategies.body: A line that enters a dot must leave it. If only one way out is left, the line goes there.

strategies.title: No small loops
strategies.body: Joining two ends of the same line closes a loop. If other lines remain, that side must stay empty.

faq.q: Can a board have more than one answer?
faq.a: No. Each board is checked by computer to have exactly one answer.

faq.q: What is 11×11?
faq.a: 11 dots a side, 10×10 cells: the same size as the board on the show.

faq.q: How do challenges and the ranking work?
faq.a: A new challenge is a fresh random 11×11 board; clear it and you own it. Anyone who clears it within the owner’s time takes it. The ranking counts the boards you own. One try per board.

WallGo2Guide.title: Wallgo II — splitting the board with square and round pieces
WallGo2Guide.intro: Wallgo II from The Devil's Plan 3 prison match, episode 10. As in Wallgo you move pieces and build walls to claim the largest territory, but there are now two kinds of piece and no staying put, so every move counts. Play 3-player or 1:1 vs AI, invite friends with a link or 4-digit code, or open a public room, and replay the game afterwards.
rules: Build walls on a 7×7 board to make your territory the largest.
Round 1 is a 3-player game. Each player gets one square and one round piece. In turn order each player places one of them on an empty tile; the second pieces go down in reverse order.
A square piece moves 1–2 tiles in one direction. A round piece moves 1 tile and may then turn left or right for 1 more tile.
On your turn you have 90 seconds to move a piece and then build a wall. You cannot move onto another piece or through a wall.
In round 1 only, each player may once knock down a wall on the path and move through it.
After moving, build a wall on one side of that piece. A side that already has a wall cannot take another; if time runs out a wall goes on a random side.
The game ends the moment every player's pieces are walled apart, even if someone never used their wall break.
Add up the tiles of the areas your pieces are in; the most wins. On a tie, the bigger single area ranks higher.
Round 2 is 1:1. The player with more territory in round 1 goes first. Each starts with 2 square and 2 round pieces, the round ones on fixed tiles. There is no wall break.

special.title: No staying put
special.body: Unlike Wallgo, you must move. A piece with nowhere to go cannot be picked, and if neither of your pieces can move, your turn is skipped.

special.title: Round pieces cannot go 2 straight
special.body: A round piece moves 1 tile and may only turn, so it ends up 1 tile away or diagonally. Two straight tiles is a square-piece move.

special.title: Wall break is on the path
special.body: You may break any one wall on the path you take, not just one next to the piece. Tiles you can only reach by breaking are shown in red.

special.title: Ties go to the big room
special.body: If two players have the same total, the size of their largest single area decides. One big room beats several small ones.

WallGo2Guide.strategyTitle: Tips — play to each piece's strength
WallGo2Guide.strategyIntro: Square pieces reach far to cut off a lane; round pieces turn corners to slip out of tight spots.

strategies.title: Round piece near the centre
strategies.body: Round pieces can turn, so they are hard to trap. Near the centre they can break out in any direction.

strategies.title: Cut lanes with the square
strategies.body: A square piece can travel two tiles straight and wall off a lane in one turn.

strategies.title: Save the break for an escape
strategies.body: You get one break. It is worth most when your piece is about to be shut in a small room and can punch through to a bigger one.

strategies.title: Guard one big room
strategies.body: Ties are settled by the largest area, so keeping one big room is safer than splitting into many.

faq.q: How is it different from Wallgo?
faq.a: There are square and round pieces that move differently, no staying put, the wall break works on the path, and ties are settled by the largest area.

faq.q: Can I play alone?
faq.a: Yes. Play 3-player against 2 AI or 1:1 against 1 AI, on easy, normal or hard. 1:1 also has Very Hard, an AI that reads several turns ahead.

faq.q: How do I play with friends?
faq.a: Create a room under Play with friends and send the link or 4-digit code. You can also open a public room in Open match.

faq.q: Where do the round pieces start in round 2?
faq.a: Each player's two round pieces start on fixed tiles facing each other diagonally; you only place the two square pieces.

MorrisGuide.title: Nine Men's Morris — mill, take, fly
MorrisGuide.intro: Nine Men's Morris is a board game from Roman times that drew new fans as the first game of the final in Netflix's The Devil's Plan season 1. Each player places and moves nine pieces on 24 points joined by three nested squares, taking an enemy piece with every line of three. The rules are short, but the fight for points while placing and the reading while moving run deep. Play it on PUZZLTHINK against the AI or with a friend by invite link or 4-digit code, best of three.
rules: The board has 24 points joined by lines. Black and white have nine pieces each; black goes first.
Placing: take turns putting one piece on an empty point. Pieces cannot move until all nine are placed.
Moving: after that, each turn move one piece one step along a line to a free neighbouring point.
Mills: three of yours on a straight line take one enemy piece. Pieces in your opponent's mills cannot be taken.
Flying: once placing is over and you are down to three pieces, you may move to any empty point.
Losing: two pieces left, or no piece that can move on your turn, loses the round.
Deadlock: once someone has three pieces, ten turns without a capture end the round; fewer pieces loses, equal is a draw.
Best of three, colours swap every round. Friend games have a 30/60/90s turn clock with an automatic move on time out.

special.title: Two mills at once
special.body: Even when one move closes two mills, you take only one piece.

special.title: Every enemy piece in a mill
special.body: As on the show, pieces in a mill are safe — if all of them are, this mill takes nothing.

special.title: Boxed in after placing
special.body: You can't get stuck while placing, but if all your pieces are blocked once placing ends, you lose on your first moving turn.

special.title: Flying needs exactly three
special.body: You fly only after placing, with exactly three pieces on the board. A flying opponent can block your mill point from anywhere.

MorrisGuide.strategyIntro: Games are won by taking good points while placing and by running mills while moving.

strategies.title: Take the junctions
strategies.body: Points with four neighbours (D6, B4, F4, D2) are the most flexible once moving starts. Take them before rushing a mill.

strategies.title: Don't get boxed in
strategies.body: If nothing can move when placing ends, you lose. Don't crowd your pieces into corners surrounded by enemy pieces.

strategies.title: Run a mill
strategies.body: Step one piece out of a mill and back in on your next turn to take a piece every time — as long as your opponent cannot fill the gap.

strategies.title: Double mill
strategies.body: Set up a piece that closes one mill or the other every time it moves, and there is no defence.

strategies.title: Block two-in-a-row
strategies.body: Two enemy pieces on a line with the third point free is a mill next turn. Block it, especially while placing.

strategies.title: Fly to block
strategies.body: With three pieces you can block a mill point anywhere. But with the ten-turn deadlock rule, time isn't on your side if you have fewer pieces.

faq.a: On PUZZLTHINK's Nine Men's Morris page, in any PC or mobile browser, with no sign-up or install.

faq.a: Yes: nine pieces, pieces in mills are safe, fly with three, lose with two, a 10-turn deadlock with three left goes to the side with more pieces, best of three. Instead of piece benefits, colours swap each round.

faq.q: How strong is the AI?
faq.a: Easy slips now and then, normal looks three moves ahead, hard five or more. Beat hard to earn a hard-clear certificate.

FlipOmokGuide.title: Flip Omok — sandwich, flip, make exactly five
FlipOmokGuide.intro: Flip Omok is an original board game by the PUZZLTHINK developer: Omok with Othello’s flip. You still race to five in a row, but any enemy stones you close between two of yours flip to your colour. A line you thought was blocked can turn over in one move, and a blocker can end up in your opponent’s line. Play COCO (Medium or Hard) or a friend by link or 4-digit code.
rules: Red (first) and blue take turns placing one stone on the points of a 15×15 board.
When your new stone and another of your stones close a straight run of enemy stones, every stone in that run flips to your colour. All 8 directions count, at any length.
★ Only the player who moves flips. A stone placed between two enemy stones stays yours, so cutting into their line is a solid defence.
Exactly five of your colour in a row wins. Stones flipped earlier count, but a five that includes a stone flipped by that move does not. Six or more does not win.
Double threes (two open threes at once) are forbidden for both sides, unless the move completes five.
A full board is a draw. Friend games have a turn clock (15, 30 or 60s); a move is made for you when it runs out, and three in a row lose.

special.title: Several directions at once
special.body: If one move closes runs in several directions, all of them flip together.

special.title: No five by flipping
special.body: If a flip lines up five of your colour, it doesn’t win when a stone flipped by that move is in the five. Flipped stones count as yours from the next move.

special.title: Flipped stones can flip back
special.body: A flipped stone can be sandwiched again. Its eye colour just marks that it has been flipped before.

special.title: Six doesn’t count
special.body: Six or more in a row, flipped or not, isn’t a win — you can even defend by turning their five into six.

FlipOmokGuide.strategyIntro: Seeing what can be sandwiched matters as much as Omok skill.

strategies.title: Block close, then check
strategies.body: A blocker right next to their line can flip, but a five made by that flip doesn’t win. Once flipped it counts for them from the next move, so block that line’s end again. Block with your own stone or the edge behind you and it can’t flip.

strategies.title: Revive a blocked line
strategies.body: A single enemy stone capping your line is an opening: place beyond it and it becomes yours, extending the line.

strategies.title: Double threats by flipping
strategies.body: A move that flips and makes a new four at once is hard to answer — even Hard COCO struggles with it.

strategies.title: Use the ✕
strategies.body: A ✕ point is somewhere your opponent can’t block. Steer your attack through it.

faq.q: Do you pass when you can’t flip, like Othello?
faq.a: No. Any empty point is legal, flip or not — except a double-three (✕) point.

faq.q: Why red and blue instead of black and white?
faq.a: So flipped stones can show the other colour in their eyes: a blue stone with red eyes used to be red.

faq.q: Are restrictions black-only, like Renju?
faq.a: No. The double-three ban and the six-doesn’t-count rule apply to both sides.

faq.q: Are results recorded?
faq.a: Yes. AI and friend games go to your records.

FlipOmokGuide.disclaimer: Flip Omok is an original game with rules made by PUZZLTHINK.

MonorailGuide.title: Monorail — win the fight for the final tile
MonorailGuide.intro: Monorail is a two-player spatial strategy game about building one closed line from sixteen straight-or-corner tiles. Because rails may mismatch until the end, count both remaining tiles and viable space.
rules: Start with two station tiles and sixteen rail tiles.
Alternate turns placing one to three tiles; multiple tiles form one straight contiguous line.
The group must touch the layout orthogonally, though its rail ends need not match yet.
The last player to make every tile one station loop wins.
Impossible may be called only before placing; the challenged player wins by finishing the loop and loses by giving up.

special.title: Must all sixteen be used?
special.body: No. You may finish earlier, but every tile already on the table must belong to the final loop.

special.title: May rail ends mismatch?
special.body: Yes during play. Position is checked immediately; rail continuity is checked only when a completed loop is claimed.

special.title: When can I call Impossible?
special.body: Only at the untouched start of your own turn.

special.title: How do I answer an Impossible call?
special.body: You may place the remaining tiles on any empty cells, with no one-to-three limit or straight-line rule. Tap a placed tile with another face selected to change it, or with the same face to remove it. Submit unlocks once every tile on the table forms one loop.

special.title: What if I gave up but a loop existed?
special.body: The caller still wins: as on the show, only a loop actually built counts. The result screen shows a possible completion as translucent gold tiles.

special.title: All sixteen tiles are down and there's no loop?
special.body: No tiles remain, so the next player may declare Impossible, and since completion truly is impossible, that player wins. Check your last placement carefully.

MonorailGuide.strategyIntro: Monorail has no luck and no hidden information, so in theory one side has a forced win. Published analysis counts roughly 150 distinct first moves for the first player, ignoring symmetry. Only about five of them win; after any other first move the second player wins. The game is a first-player win on paper, but without knowing the exact opening it becomes a reading battle to the end. The principles below prevent most early mistakes.

strategies.title: A finished loop always has an even length
strategies.body: A closed path on a grid must undo every horizontal and vertical step, so its length is even. Without the two stations, a finished loop uses 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 or 16 rail tiles. Any detour also adds exactly two cells. Every tile count starts from this fact.

strategies.title: The shortest finish is six tiles
strategies.body: Step out of each station's outer end, turn down (or up) and meet: that 2×4 ring is the shortest loop and needs six rail tiles. Early on, don't leave its cells open so that your opponent can fill them in two turns.

strategies.title: At least four curves, and each curve commits
strategies.body: A closed loop has exactly four more outward corners than inward ones, so it needs at least four curves. A curve fixes two directions the loop must take. That makes it a far stronger restriction on your opponent than a straight.

strategies.title: Never hand over a straight gap of three or less
strategies.body: You may place up to three tiles in one line, so whoever moves when the missing cells form a straight run of three or fewer wins. After your move, the missing cells should bend or number four or more, so your opponent cannot finish in one go.

strategies.title: Use a detour to flip the count
strategies.body: If the endgame count favours your opponent, push the loop outward and add two missing cells. While tiles remain, a detour is the only way to change the count. Once the supply runs low, detours disappear too.

strategies.title: Mirroring is not a forced win
strategies.body: Copying your opponent symmetrically around the stations feels safe, but it isn't. A mirrored loop grows on both sides and quickly breaks the sixteen-tile limit, and a cell on the axis of symmetry breaks the pairing. The opening famously recommended on the show was not actually a winning move.

strategies.title: Check Impossible at the start of every turn
strategies.body: You can declare only before selecting a tile. So first ask: does a loop through every tile on the table still fit within the remaining supply? If your opponent left a dead-end curve or a misaligned straight, declare and win. If your own move makes completion impossible, your opponent declares next turn.

strategies.title: Second player: stay wide. First player: stay exact
strategies.body: The first player only has to follow the correct line. The second player is waiting for a slip. Keep several possible routes alive to make the counting hard, and strike when the opponent misjudges the endgame.

faq.q: Can I play online with a friend?
faq.a: Yes. Use an invite link or four-digit code, or join a signed-in open 1v1 room.

faq.q: How do the AI levels differ?
faq.a: Medium mixes its best route with mistakes. Hard samples more completion routes and follows the multiple-of-four endgame more often.

faq.q: What happens when Impossible is called?
faq.a: Just like the show: the opponent must finish the loop with the remaining tiles. Finish it and they win; give up and the caller wins. Call it on the AI and it either completes the loop on the spot or concedes.

faq.q: Is there a forced win?
faq.a: Published analysis finds about five winning first moves among roughly 150 distinct ones (ignoring symmetry); every other opening is a second-player win. You need the exact opening and the follow-up, so in practice tile counting (parity, the three-cell finish) and route flexibility decide games.

special.title: Two lines at once?

FourThreeGuide.strategyIntro: It is all about balancing defence and your own score. Ally AIs chase gems too, so block the Guest without giving up your own chances.

strategies.title: Cover a Guest pair at once
strategies.body: When the Guest has two in a line, take the open cell or stack on top of a Guest piece. Covering is the surest block.

strategies.title: Remember what is under you
strategies.body: Don't move a piece sitting on a Guest piece lightly: lifting it may open a Guest line.

strategies.title: Take the centre four
strategies.body: The centre cells sit on the most lines. With stacking, covering the centre is strong too.

strategies.title: Make a double threat
strategies.body: One move that sets up two lines at once is hard to stop. Moves that create a fork work especially well.

strategies.title: Keep pieces in hand
strategies.body: A new piece can go anywhere, which makes it your best block. Spend them all early and you can only shuffle later.

strategies.title: Don't forget the gem race
strategies.body: Every round an ally AI takes pushes you away from the final. Look for moves that block and build your own line at the same time.

faq.q: What is 4 Player 3 In a Row?

faq.q: Who is the Special Guest?
faq.a: The opponent everyone must stop, always played by an AI. Unlike the show, PUZZLTHINK reveals the Guest's colour at the start and marks its pieces with a star (★).

faq.q: Can I choose the AI level?
faq.a: No. Ally and Guest AIs always play their best move, so you never lose to an AI blunder: play well and you win, slip and you lose.

faq.q: How many friends do I need?
faq.a: Two or three people. With two, an ally AI fills the third seat; the Guest is always an AI. Invite by link or 4-digit code.

faq.q: What counts as a win?
faq.a: Completing the mission (players win all four rounds) and going through to the final (top two by gems).

Merge2048Guide.title: 2048 — a calm number puzzle, from square to stone
Merge2048Guide.intro: 2048 is a puzzle where you slide matching number blocks together to make bigger numbers. The rules take a minute to learn, but how you keep the board tidy makes all the difference. PUZZLTHINK's 2048 draws every block as a character with a face: small numbers are squares, from 128 they grow into shiny stones, and 2048 wears a crown. Play at your own pace in free play, go for the ranking in an challenge run, or race friends live.
rules: The board has 4×4 = 16 cells. It starts with two blocks, each a 2 or a 4.
Push up, down, left or right and every block slides that way until it can go no further.
When two blocks with the same number meet they merge into one worth double, and the new number is added to your score.
A block merges only once per move: 2·2·2·2 pushed left becomes 4·4, not 8.
If anything moved, a new block (a 2 at 90 %, a 4 at 10 %) appears in an empty cell. A push that moves nothing does nothing.
With no empty cell and no equal neighbours left, the game is over.

special.title: Block characters and a collection
special.body: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 are pastel square characters; 128, 256, 512 and 1024 are stones. From 2048 every block is a crowned legend: the gold stone at 2048, the black stone king at 4096 (silver crown, starlight), the white stone king at 8192 (gold crown, halo), the aurora stone at 16384 (jewelled crown), and a cosmic stone beyond. Every block you have ever made fills in your collection.

special.title: Free play is the relaxed mode
special.body: No clock, one-step undo, and the board saves itself so you can come back later. The soft merge sound can be turned off at the top right.

special.title: Challenge-run ranking
special.body: No clock: one board goes on until no move is left, and that score goes on the 2048 ranking. No undo, but the board saves itself, so a reload or a later visit picks up where you left off. Starting over gives up the run in progress without recording it.

special.title: Live friend race
special.body: 2–4 players start from the same seed, so the blocks come in the same order for everyone. Your board shows big and your friends' small, live; after 5 or 10 minutes the biggest block wins, and level blocks go to the higher score.

Merge2048Guide.strategyTitle: Tips — pick one corner as home
Merge2048Guide.strategyIntro: Most people who reach the big numbers play the same way. The key is never to scatter the board.

strategies.title: Keep the biggest block in a corner
strategies.body: Choose a corner, say bottom-left, and keep your biggest block there. Use the direction that pulls it out of the corner (up, in this case) only when you must.

strategies.title: Line up one row by size
strategies.body: Keep the corner row in order, like 512·256·128·64. Merges then chain from the end and build a big block in one go.

strategies.title: Use mostly two directions
strategies.body: Alternate between two directions such as left and down, and use a third only now and then. Using all four drags the big blocks into the middle.

strategies.title: The board before the clock
strategies.body: In a friend race, not getting stuck matters more than pushing fast. A stuck board freezes your result, so take risks only when time is nearly up.

faq.q: Where can I play 2048?

faq.q: Does the game end at 2048?

faq.q: How do I play with friends?

faq.q: Is the friend race fair?
faq.a: Yes. Everyone starts from the same seed, so the first board and the order of new blocks are the same; only your moves make the boards differ.

faq.q: Where are my records kept?
faq.a: Signed in, your challenge-run scores go on the 2048 ranking and the challenge ranking in Records, and friend and open matches go into your match history. Your free-play best is kept in this browser.

PointOmokGuide.title: Point Omok rules and strategy
PointOmokGuide.intro: Point Omok is an unofficial fan-made web version of the final match of the exile in Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). Instead of taking turns placing stones, each round three points are put up and both players bid for them in secret; the higher bid takes the point. It is gomoku plus bidding psychology and point management. Play it against the AI, or 1:1 with a friend by invite link, 4-digit code or open room.
rules: Two players on a 15×15 board repeat choose → bid → place every round.
Within 90 seconds the chooser puts up three empty points in a row (across, down or diagonal). The first chooser is random; from round 2 the players take turns.
Both players get 10 points every round and split them over the three points within 90 seconds: at least 1 on each, whole numbers only.
Each point gets the stone of whoever bid more on it. On a tie, the player who did not choose this round gets it.
Only half of the points you keep (rounded down) carry over to the next round.
Once all three stones are down, a player with a five wins. If both have one, more fives wins; the same number is a draw.
Only exactly five counts. Six or more in a row (an overline) is not a five, so adding a stone to a five takes it away. If no three empty points in a row are left, it is a draw.

special.title: The three stones land together
special.body: All three stones go down at once and their order means nothing. If both players make a five in the same round, it is decided by how many fives, not by who was first.

special.title: Ties go to the non-chooser
special.body: The chooser picks where, but loses ties. If you put up your own winning point, you have to bid clearly more than the other player.

special.title: The other player's points are hidden
special.body: You never see how much the other player bid or kept. You can only work it out from past results; every bid is shown when the game ends.

special.title: When time runs out
special.body: Out of time choosing, three points next to the stones are picked for you; out of time bidding, whatever is on your steppers is locked. In a friend game, a bid that never arrives counts as 1·1·1.

PointOmokGuide.strategyIntro: In Point Omok, when to bid matters as much as where. Here are common ideas.

strategies.title: Save on quiet rounds
strategies.body: Bid just 1·1·1 on a round that decides nothing, keep 7 and carry 3. Save for a few rounds and you can clearly outbid the other player when it counts.

strategies.title: Put your winning point in the line
strategies.body: As the chooser, include a point where you can make five. The other player must bid big to stop it, which makes the other two points cheap.

strategies.title: Count their points
strategies.body: A point they took means they bid at least as much as you. With 10 a round and half of the rest carried over, past results tell you their most possible points quite exactly.

strategies.title: Pile on or spread out
strategies.body: Piling on one point nearly secures it but gives up the other two. Read where they want to win, and put just 1 on the point they want least.

faq.q: What is Point Omok?

ColorLinkDuelGuide.title: Color Link Duel rules and strategy — The Devil's Plan 3 final, match 2
ColorLinkDuelGuide.intro: Color Link Duel was the second match of the final in Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). Two players take turns placing colored stones, and the board must always stay joinable: every same-colored pair connected without lines crossing. Leave a board that cannot be joined and you get called out; make a wrong call and you lose instead. On PUZZLTHINK you can play it 1:1 on 13 boards against the AI, a friend or an open room.
rules: There are 13 boards: the classic 7×7 and 12 shaped boards such as the heart, the donut, four rooms and the stairs. Each is rated Easy, Normal or Hard; pick one or go random.
There are 14 colors from A to N, two stones each, 28 in all. The players take turns placing them.
The opener places one stone; after that each turn is two stones of different colors within one minute. Miss the clock and you lose the round.
If every same-colored pair on the board were joined by a line, no two lines may cross or share a cell, and each line must be at least 6 cells long, stones included.
A color with only one stone down must still be joinable to a partner placed later.
Think the board your opponent just made cannot be joined? Call it impossible on your turn. They get 2 minutes to draw every line: prove it and they win, fail and you do.
You choose to go first or second (in rooms a coin toss picks who chooses). On PUZZLTHINK one round decides the match: the first point wins.

special.title: A color with one stone
special.body: A color without its partner yet must still have room for one: some empty cell where the partner could go and be joined with a line of 6 or more. If that stone gets boxed in, the board is impossible.

special.title: The 6-cell rule
special.body: Line length counts both end stones. Two stones of a color placed close together must loop around to reach 6 cells, so a tight pair can eat a surprising amount of space.

special.title: A wrong call
special.body: If the called player draws every line within 2 minutes, the proof stands and the caller loses. If they cannot draw it in time, the caller wins, even if the board could in fact be joined.

special.title: Shaped boards with walls
special.body: Stones and lines cannot use the walls of a shaped board. Boards with narrow corridors and dead ends tangle lines easily, which is why they are rated Hard.

ColorLinkDuelGuide.strategyIntro: The game is about never breaking the board yourself while handing your opponent a board they will break. Check that the board still joins after every move, and shrink the room they have for their next two stones.

strategies.title: Join it once before you play
strategies.body: Before placing your two stones, trace every color's line in your head. If your board is already impossible, you lose the moment your opponent calls it.

strategies.title: Split the big open areas
strategies.body: Wide open space is where your opponent can play safely. Place stones on the chokepoints lines must pass through and the safe spots run out quickly.

strategies.title: Tie up lone stones
strategies.body: A color with one stone needs a path left for its partner. Play other colors near that path and your opponent spends their turns keeping it open.

strategies.title: Call impossible only when sure
strategies.body: A wrong call loses on the spot. Call it when you see a clear reason: two colors that must share one corridor, or a boxed-in stone that cannot reach 6 cells.

strategies.title: When called, draw from the edges
strategies.body: In the 2-minute proof, start with lines in corners and dead ends. Fixing the lines that have only one route makes the rest fall into place.

strategies.title: Learn on the easy boards
strategies.body: Wide boards like four rooms, the donut, the frame and the pillars leave room to recover from mistakes. Once lines come naturally, try the Hard boards: classic, heart, diamond.

faq.q: What are the rules of Color Link Duel from The Devil's Plan 3 final?
faq.a: Two players take turns placing stones of 14 colors (two each), keeping the board joinable: same colors connected by lines of 6 cells or more that never cross. Think the board cannot be joined? Call it impossible; if your opponent cannot prove otherwise in 2 minutes, you win.

faq.q: How is it different from the solo Color Link puzzle?
faq.a: Color Link is a puzzle where you join given dots on your own. Color Link Duel is a two-player game where you take turns placing stones and push each other toward a board that cannot be joined.

faq.q: How do the board difficulties differ?
faq.a: Wide open boards (four rooms, donut, frame, pillars) are Easy, boards with corridors (stairs, H, zigzag, arrow) are Normal, and tight boards (classic, heart, diamond, cross, hourglass) are Hard. The AI plays the same; the board sets the difficulty.

faq.q: Can I play with friends?
faq.a: Yes. Invite a friend with a link or 4-digit code, or join an open room to play someone 1:1. The host picks the board or leaves it random.

CardJanggiGuide.title: Card Janggi rules and strategy — The Devil's Plan 3 final, match 1
CardJanggiGuide.intro: Card Janggi was match 1 of the final in Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). Pieces move as in janggi or chess, but which move you get is set in advance by the secret order of your five movement cards. Your opponent's next card is face up and the rest are hidden, so you play two battles at once: the move now and the order of your cards. On PUZZLTHINK you can play it by the show's rules against a hard AI, a friend or an open-room opponent.
rules: Two players on a 6×5 board. Each has one king and three small pieces, set out on the same starting squares as on the show.

Five movement cards, the same for both: Rat (1 step orthogonally), Horse (a chess knight's jump), Monkey (1 step any direction), Elephant (a bishop slide until blocked) and Giraffe (a jump of exactly 2 orthogonally).
On PUZZLTHINK you choose to go first or second: against the AI you pick, in friend and open rooms a coin toss picks who chooses.
At the start of a round both lay out their cards face down. The first player uses all five; the second player picks four of five (first cycle only). The first cards are turned up together.
Turns alternate from the first player: move any one piece as the face-up card allows, then turn up your next card. Moving onto an enemy piece takes it; you cannot move onto your own.

When you use your last card, you lay out all five again right away and turn up only the first. So the second player re-lays first, and the first player sees that new first card before using their last one.
90 seconds per move. If you do not play your card in time, your opponent moves one of your pieces with it.
Take the enemy king, or move your king onto the square the enemy king started on, to win the round. On PUZZLTHINK one round decides the match.

special.title: No legal move
special.body: If the face-up card cannot move any of your pieces, it is used up without a move. The show never hit this case; this is PUZZLTHINK's call.

special.title: Giraffe and elephant
special.body: The giraffe jumps over anything to the square exactly two away. The elephant slides diagonally and stops at the first piece, which it may take if it is an enemy.

special.title: The second player's four cards
special.body: Only in the first cycle does the second player use four of five. That puts them one move ahead in the cycle, and from then on the 'see their new first card before your last card' rhythm keeps going.

special.title: Rounds that do not end
special.body: Past 60 moves in a round, the side with more pieces wins; with equal pieces it is a drawn round, which counts for nobody (at most five rounds).

CardJanggiGuide.strategyIntro: Your opponent's next card is always visible, and you can count which cards they have left. Start from those two facts: work out every square they can reach next move.

strategies.title: Keep your king out of their face-up card's reach
strategies.body: If any enemy piece can land on your king with their face-up card, move it or block now. Check whole diagonals for the elephant and all eight L-squares for the horse.

strategies.title: Order your cards two moves ahead
strategies.body: Your first card plays on today's board; your second plays where the first one leaves you. Keep flexible cards such as the monkey for later and put the giraffe or elephant up front only when you can see a clear use.

strategies.title: The card you leave out is a weapon
strategies.body: Going second, you drop one card in the first cycle. Drop the one least useful on this board, and use the earlier re-layout to press on your opponent's last card.

strategies.title: Block paths and your home square
strategies.body: You lose if their king reaches your king's starting square. A small piece near that square blocks the way in or takes the king that tries to enter.

strategies.title: Count their cards
strategies.body: No card repeats within a cycle. Strike out what they have used and their next options shrink; the last one or two cards are almost certain.

strategies.title: Time your last card
strategies.body: Going first, you play your last card after seeing their new first card. A finishing card at the end of your layout lets you strike knowing how they can answer.

faq.q: What are the rules of Card Janggi from The Devil's Plan 3 final?
faq.a: On a 6×5 board each side has one king and three small pieces and moves only as its secret order of five cards (rat, horse, monkey, elephant, giraffe) allows. Take the enemy king or reach its starting square to win the round, and one round wins the match.

faq.q: What was the final of The Devil's Plan: Dead Again?
faq.a: Card Janggi was match 1 of the season 3 final. This page is an unofficial fan-made web version you can play against the AI or a friend.

faq.q: How do first and second player differ?
faq.a: The first player uses all five cards; the second uses four of five in the first cycle. After that both use five, and whoever plays their last card re-lays at once and turns up the first. You choose first or second (in rooms a coin toss picks who chooses).

faq.q: What happens on a timeout?
faq.a: If you do not play your card within 90 seconds, your opponent moves your piece with it (the AI picks against the AI; in rooms your opponent has 20 seconds). Three time-outs in a row lose the match.

faq.q: Does the AI see my card order?
faq.a: No. It sees exactly what you would: your used cards and your face-up next card. It weighs every order your hidden cards could be in and plays the best move on average.

faq.q: How do I play with a friend?
faq.a: Create a 1:1 room and send the link or the 4-digit code. Open rooms match you with anyone, and results go into the records rankings.

GradationGuide.title: Gradation online — The Devil's Plan 3 prison match in your browser
GradationGuide.intro: Gradation is a 1:1 mind game: secretly share seven number cubes among your cups, then hand the cups in one at a time to see whose number is bigger. The cups are dark at both ends and lighter toward the middle, so the dark cup your opponent hands in could hold their smallest number — or their largest. It comes from the day-6 prison match (the way to the final) of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3), with the show's rules, four AI players with different styles (all hard), friend rooms and open 1:1 rooms.
rules: Each player gets seven shaded cups (dark · grey · light · white · light · grey · dark) and twenty number cubes (0–9, two of each).
Within 5 minutes, secretly put one cube in each cup. Numbers must rise (or stay equal) from left to right, and the seven must add up to 30 or less.
The lead player hands in one cup. The opponent sees only its shade, never which place it came from. Then the opponent hands in one cup.
Both cubes are shown; the higher number wins the round and 1 point. A tie changes nothing.
The winner of a round leads the next one; after a tie the lead stays.
After seven rounds the higher score wins. On a tie both players place new rows and play again until someone wins.

special.title: Every shade comes in a pair
special.body: Dark cups are places 1 and 7, grey 2 and 6, light 3 and 5. Because the row rises, one dark cup holds the smallest number and the other the largest. Only the white cup (place 4) is single, so it gives away the middle number.

special.title: You may repeat a number
special.body: There are two cubes of each number, so 4 · 4 side by side is fine (equal counts as rising). Three of the same is not possible.

special.title: 30 or less — but use it all
special.body: A sum under 30 is legal, but a bigger cube is never worse than a smaller one, so strong rows use the full 30.

special.title: A decided match ends at once
special.body: When one side leads by more than the rounds left, the match ends right there (how this web version plays).

GradationGuide.strategyTitle: Strategy — read the shade, give up cheaply
GradationGuide.strategyIntro: The only thing your opponent ever sees is a shade. What you show and what you hide decides the match.

strategies.title: Two sacrifice cubes
strategies.body: You only need four of seven rounds. Rows that throw away two or three small cubes (0 · 0 or 0 · 1) and pile the rest on the top four or five — like 0 · 0 · 1 · 3 · 8 · 9 · 9 — are strong.

strategies.title: A dark cup is an extreme
strategies.body: A dark cup holds your opponent's smallest or largest cube. Combine the numbers already shown with the 30 limit and you can often tell which.

strategies.title: If you cannot win, lose small
strategies.body: If their cup looks big, answer with your smallest cube and keep the big ones for rounds you can take. Losing rounds cheaply is the whole game.

strategies.title: Leading gives information
strategies.body: The lead shows a shade first, which can be a disadvantage. Use dark cups to keep them guessing, and the white cup when you want them to spend a big cube.

strategies.title: Four AI styles
strategies.body: Nova (calculator) plays only the likeliest win, Rex (aggressor) leads with big cubes, Miro (wall) builds an even row for the middle rounds, and Jude (trickster) bluffs with dark cups. None peeks at your row: each plays out hundreds of imagined matches from the shades and numbers shown so far.

strategies.title: The Gradation champion badge
strategies.body: The #1 of the AI Hall of Fame wears the gradation crown. When the ranking changes, the badge moves to the new #1 automatically.

faq.q: What is Gradation?
faq.a: A 1:1 number mind game from the day-6 prison match of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). Hide seven cubes in shaded cups, rising and summing to 30 or less, then duel one cup at a time seeing only shades; win more rounds to win.

faq.q: How is it different from the show?
faq.a: On the show you needed two wins in a row to reach the final. Here it is a single match (seven rounds, rematch on a tie), with 5 minutes to place and a random first lead.

faq.q: How strong is the AI?
faq.a: There is only a hard level. The AI never looks at your row: it weighs every row that fits the shades and numbers shown so far, plays hundreds of imagined matches, and hands in the cup most likely to win. One of four styles is drawn each match.

faq.q: Can I play with friends?
faq.a: Yes. Create a friend room and send the link or 4-digit code for a 1:1 match, or list it as an open room. Rows and handed-in cups reach the other side end-to-end encrypted and stay hidden until shown.

faq.q: Where are my records?
faq.a: Signed in, AI wins count for the Hall of Fame and the hard-clear certificate, and friend/open matches for the open ranking. The AI #1 wears the Gradation champion badge.

HiddenWordGuide.title: Hidden Word online — The Devil's Plan 3 episode 5 main match, the similarity word game
HiddenWordGuide.intro: Hidden Word is a word duel run by one number: similarity. The setter gives words related to a hidden word, and each hint shows how close it is, from 0 to 100%. This version is based on the episode 5 main match of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3) and plays as a one-on-one point match against the AI MORA, taking turns to set and to guess. The words are Korean.
rules: A match is two rounds. Each round you set once (defense) and guess MORA's word once (attack); the order is drawn at random.
At the start you pick one of six envelopes holding five common nouns. One is your hidden word in round 1, one of the other four in round 2.
Hints: the setter gives Korean nouns. Each hint shows its similarity to the hidden word, and a hint at 95% or more ends the hint phase at once.
A stage allows five hints and two minutes. If none reaches 95%, the word closest to the hidden word is revealed instead.
Answers: when the hints end the other side answers. A miss pays the setter and starts the next stage, up to three: 1, 2, then 3 points.
The guesser earns more the earlier the answer: 6, 3, then 1. Once per word a chance lets you write a second answer.
Round 2 doubles every point. The ranking score is your average points per match plus 0.3 per match played (up to 20).

special.title: Low hints are shown too
special.body: A word you hoped was 95% but scored 80% still goes on the board. Every hint is a clue, so lead with the ones you are sure of.

special.title: Wrong answers show their similarity
special.body: Yours and MORA's. A wrong answer at 88% says the word is a close relative.

special.title: The hidden word itself is not a hint
special.body: A compound containing it is allowed, but it gives the answer away.

special.title: Out of time, the closest word is revealed
special.body: After five hints or two minutes, the closest word on the association list is shown and the other side answers.

HiddenWordGuide.strategyIntro: MORA does not read a score table: she picks the word that best fits the meaning of the hints. Play her like a person and confuse her.

strategies.title: Pick hints that fit several words
strategies.body: For 포도 (grape), 와인 (wine) passes 95% but points to one answer. 과일 (fruit) fits apple, strawberry and watermelon just as well.

strategies.title: Words with two meanings are shields
strategies.body: 배 (pear, ship, belly) or 눈 (eye, snow) can pass 95% with a hint from the other meaning, sending the guess to the wrong family.

strategies.title: Low hints give the direction
strategies.body: Look at where the 78% and 85% hints point together, not just at the 96% one. MORA's hints narrow down stage by stage.

strategies.title: Spend the chance in stage 2
strategies.body: Stage 1 has too many candidates and stage 3 pays 1. With two candidates left in stage 2 the chance is worth the most.

faq.q: Which show is Hidden Word from?
faq.a: It is the episode 5 main match of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). This is an unofficial fan-made version rebuilt as a one-on-one point match against an AI.

faq.q: How is similarity computed?
faq.a: From precomputed word vectors (how often words appear together and how close their meanings are), dictionary relations, and an association list written for each hidden word, blended into 0–100%. No AI model is called during play.

faq.q: Which words can I give?
faq.a: Korean words without spaces, up to eight syllables: about 74,000 nouns and noun forms.

faq.q: Does MORA know my word?
faq.a: No. She sees only the hints and their numbers and reasons from how related words are. Her own word never leaves the server before the turn ends.

faq.q: How does the ranking work?
faq.a: The ranking score is your average points per match plus a bonus for matches played. A perfect match is 36 points; the bonus is 0.3 per finished match up to 20 matches (at most +6). For example, an average of 19.5 over 6 matches is 19.5 + 1.8 = 21.3. Skill sets the order and steady play is still rewarded. You are ranked once you finish 3 matches while signed in.

faq.q: Can I play with friends?
faq.a: Only the AI point match is open for now.

HitStayGuide.title: Hit,Stay online — The Devil's Plan 3 semifinal main match in your browser
HitStayGuide.intro: Hit,Stay is a five-player betting card game: bring the total of your number cards as close as you can to a limit set by an eight-sided die, and bet chips to survive. Every round you decide whether to take one more card (HIT), stop (STAY) and how much to risk. It recreates the semifinal main match of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3) with the show's rules, against four AI players, with friends or in open rooms.
rules: 35 number cards: one 7, two 6s, three 5s, four 4s, five 3s, six 2s, seven 1s and seven -1s.

Five players start with 30 chips each. The ante is 1 chip and goes up by 1 every 2 rounds (1, 1, 2, 2, … 8), then by 5 every 2 rounds from round 17 (13, 13, 18, …). It is never more than the smallest stack can pay.
Each round the dealer rolls an eight-sided die (5–12) for the limit. Everyone gets three cards and shows one of them.
From the first player: bet (call, raise or fold). Nobody may put in more than the smallest stack at the table.
Then, from the first player, HIT (take a face-up card) or STAY. When everyone has stayed or the deck runs out, there is a second betting round.
Cards are revealed: the total closest to the limit takes the pot; on equal totals more cards wins; over the limit is last.
A player at 0 chips is out. The last one standing wins the main match.

special.title: There are seven -1 cards
special.body: Even over the limit, a -1 can bring you back in. Right on the limit, a -1 moves you away again: check what is left before you hit.

special.title: Equal totals go to more cards
special.body: With limit 9, 5+4 (two cards) loses to 3+3+2+1 (four cards).

special.title: Bets are capped by the smallest stack
special.body: If the shortest stack has 5 chips, nobody can put in more than 5 this round.

special.title: Ties split the pot
special.body: Same total and same number of cards: the pot is split, and odd chips go to the tied player nearest the first player.

HitStayGuide.strategyIntro: It looks like luck, but counting the visible cards changes your odds a lot.

strategies.title: Count the bust chance
strategies.body: Take the visible cards out of the 35 and you know the chance the next card takes you over.

strategies.title: Which card you show matters
strategies.body: Your face-up card is the others' clue to your total: show a big card to look strong, a small one to look weak.

strategies.title: Chips are your life
strategies.body: At 0 chips you are out. Folding a doubtful hand often beats calling close to all-in.

strategies.title: A big raise means a strong hand
strategies.body: Use the face-up cards and the hits to narrow down the raiser's total. The Hands button replays every move of the round.

faq.q: What is Hit,Stay?
faq.a: A five-player betting card game from the semifinal main match of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). Get closest to the limit and outlast the others.

faq.q: Can I play alone?
faq.a: Yes, against four AI players, all at full strength.

faq.q: Can I play with friends?
faq.a: Create a room for a link and a 4-digit code; play 1:1 up to five, and the host chooses whether AI fills the empty seats. Open rooms are listed for anyone.

faq.q: Is there a time limit?
faq.a: 10 seconds to pick your face-up card. In rooms, 30 seconds per bet or HIT/STAY; then the AI plays for you after a warning.

EquationSignalGuide.title: Equation Signal online — the Devil's Plan 3 final game, rules and tips
EquationSignalGuide.intro: Equation Signal is the third game of the final of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again. A 9-cell equation is hidden, and the green, yellow and red signal on each cell of your guess narrows it down. It plays like Nerdle, the equation version of Wordle, with powers (^) added. On PUZZLTHINK you can practise alone, take the 10-minute challenge, or race 2–4 friends in friend and open rooms.
rules: The answer has 9 cells. It may use digits 0–9 and the signs +, −, ×, ÷, = and ^ (power), any of them more than once.
The answer is a true equation with at least one equals sign. Signs never sit side by side, no number starts with 0 (like 07), and × is never left out.
A guess is free: it need not be true, need not have an equals sign and may put signs side by side, as long as all 9 cells are filled.
Each cell of a guess is coloured. Green: that symbol is in that place. Yellow: it is in the answer, in another place. Red: it is not in the answer.
If a guess uses a symbol more often than the answer does, the extra ones toward the right are red.
When all nine cells are green you win. Powers are worked out first, then × and ÷, then + and −.

special.title: Powers come first
special.body: 91^1×0 is (91^1)×0 = 0. Powers first, then × and ÷, then + and −. Stacked powers such as 2^3^2 go right to left.

special.title: Anything to the power 0 is 1
special.body: 5^0 = 1. That fact mattered in the final on the show. The equations this site makes never use confusing powers such as ^0 or ^1.

special.title: When red does not mean "none"
special.body: If you played two 3s and one came back green and one red, the answer has exactly one 3. Red also tells you there are no more.

special.title: Probing guesses are allowed
special.body: Because a guess need not be true, you can open with something like 0+−×÷12^3 to test as many signs and digits as possible. Both finalists started that way.

EquationSignalGuide.strategyIntro: One of the nine cells is always an equals sign and what is right of it is usually the result. Pin the structure first and the options shrink fast.

strategies.title: Test the signs
strategies.body: Put +, −, ×, ÷, ^ and = in your first guess to learn at once which operations are used. Fill the other three cells with different digits.

strategies.title: Sweep the other digits
strategies.body: Use the digits you have not played yet. After two guesses you know nearly every digit in the answer.

strategies.title: Find the equals sign
strategies.body: In cells 6–8 the right side is the result; in cells 4–5 both sides may be expressions (3×4=2×6). Its place is the skeleton of the equation.

strategies.title: Count the digits
strategies.body: Two digits times two digits gives three or four. Checking that the result fits the cells left removes many candidates.

strategies.title: Speed is points
strategies.body: In a room the points go by solving order. A likely candidate played early, for one more set of signals, often beats a perfect deduction.

strategies.title: Skip when stuck
strategies.body: The 10-minute challenge counts equations solved. If one has held you for two minutes, skip it and take a new one.

faq.q: What is Equation Signal?
faq.a: The third game of the final of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (The Devil's Plan 3). You find a hidden 9-cell equation; each cell of your guess lights up green, yellow or red to show how close it is.

faq.q: What do green, yellow and red mean?
faq.a: Green: that digit or sign is in that exact place. Yellow: it is in the answer but in another place. Red: it is not in the answer, or you used more copies than the answer has.

faq.q: Can I hand in an equation that is not true?
faq.a: Yes. As on the show, a guess does not have to be true and may even put signs side by side. Only the answer is a proper equation.

EquationTowerGuide.title: Tower of Equations online — the Devil's Plan 3 prison match, rules and tips
EquationTowerGuide.intro: Tower of Equations is the day-5 prison match of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again. Number blocks stand in four stacks; move and flip them until a tower of the asked height is worth the target number. On the show players buzzed with how many moves they needed and then had to do it. On PUZZLTHINK you can practise alone, take the 10-minute challenge, or play the buzzer game with 2–4 friends in friend and open rooms.
rules: Each round shows a target number (the value to reach) and a height (how many blocks the tower must have).
A move lifts any number of blocks off the top of one stack and sets them down on any stack. The bundle may be turned upside down on the way.
Turning a bundle over without moving it to another stack is a move too.
The top of the tower must be a number without a sign, and the formula runs from the top down.
In a room, buzz to offer a number of moves; the others may each make one lower offer. Only the lowest offer plays, with that many moves.
The first to buzz scores +1 for a tower and −1 for a miss. Someone who took it with a lower offer scores +2 or −2. The stacks carry over to the next round.

special.title: A plain number on top
special.body: A stack with +3 or ×2 on top is not a tower. Players on the show lost points to this rule early on.

special.title: Worked out from the top, in order
special.body: On this site each block under the top applies in turn: 5, +3, ×2 is (5+3)×2 = 16. Each stack shows its current value underneath.

special.title: The height must match exactly
special.body: The right value at the wrong height is not a finish. Spare blocks have to go to another stack.

special.title: A flip reverses the order
special.body: Flip three blocks and the top one ends up at the bottom. Use it to bring a plain number to the top or to change the order of the signs.

EquationTowerGuide.strategyIntro: Most rounds take two or three moves. Decide which plain number goes on top and the path shows itself.

strategies.title: Three candidates for the top
strategies.body: There are only three plain numbers. Pick the one that can get near the target, then look for the signed blocks to go under it.

strategies.title: Work up from the bottom block
strategies.body: The bottom block is the last operation. An even target may end in ×2; take +n off the target to see what the blocks above must make.

strategies.title: One flip saves two moves
strategies.body: If the plain number lies under a bundle, flip the whole bundle to bring it to the top in one move instead of moving blocks one by one.

strategies.title: Clearing counts too
strategies.body: A stack taller than the asked height must lose its top. If the blocks you take off finish a tower elsewhere, one move does both jobs.

strategies.title: When unsure, add one
strategies.body: A miss costs points. Undercutting pays +2 but costs −2, so offer fewer only when you see the path to the end.

strategies.title: The fewest moves score 3
strategies.body: In the 10-minute challenge the fewest moves score 3, one more 2, anything else 1. If you wandered, go back to the round start and try for the best.

faq.q: What is Tower of Equations?
faq.a: The day-5 prison match of Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (The Devil's Plan 3). You move and stack number blocks into a tower worth a target number; on the show whoever offered the fewest moves had to do it.

faq.q: What blocks are there?
faq.a: This site uses nine: three plain numbers and six signed blocks (two +, two −, one ×, one ÷). Every block carries one of four primes (2, 3, 5, 7), and towers are 3 to 5 blocks high. The show did not publish its exact set, so this one is our own.

faq.q: In what order is the tower worked out?
faq.a: From the plain number on top, down, one block at a time. It is not the usual times-before-plus order: each block applies in turn, like a pocket calculator.

faq.q: Can I play alone?
faq.a: Yes: practice with no clock, and a 10-minute challenge for points. After each round you see the fewest moves possible.

faq.q: Is it free? Do I need an account?
faq.a: It is free and needs no account. Sign in to put your 10-minute challenge on the ranking; the #1 gets the Tower of Equations icon.
